utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please call the case, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-98-29/1T, the Prosecutor versus Dragomir Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May we have the appearances.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. We have quite a few people here today. To my left is Mr. Stefan Waespi. Behind me is Ms. Carolyn Edgerton. To my right is Ms. Maxine Marcus, Mr. Manoj Sachdeva. Our case manager is Ms. Jasmina Bosnjakovic. And my name is Alex Whiting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I am Branislav Tapuskovic, attorney-at-law from Belgrade. I am Defence counsel for Mr. Dragomir Milosevic. On my right is my colleague, an attorney-at-law from Paris, who is my co-counsel. And on my left is Ms. Ruzica Jovanovic, our legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Whiting, we'll hear your opening address.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I will be doing just part of the opening address, just the beginning, and Mr. Stefan Waespi will be doing the better part of the second half of it. Mr. President, Your Honours, distinguished counsel for the Defence, this is a case of the city of Sarajevo and its people that was kept under siege, a blockade, for 44 months, the last 15 months of which were under the direction of the accused in this case, Dragomir Milosevic. It is a case of a city that was exposed to a relentless military campaign of shelling and sniping against its civilian population by a superior military force that surrounded it on the higher points. It is a case of a city whose people were constantly terrorised as they were exposed to a calculated, modulated campaign of sniping and shelling, the primary purpose of which was to inflict terror. The campaign of shelling and sniping was modulated so that firing could be increased or decreased at unpredictable times, thus subjecting the civilian population to severe psychological trauma. No one knew of any place in the city that was safe for themselves for their families or friends, regardless of gender, age, or ethnicity. Every day, civilian activity, such as gardening in one's home, shopping at the market, or riding the tram, was a hazardous endeavour, potentially subject to a barrage of shells and bullets from the besieging forces. This is a trial ultimately of the accused, General Dragomir Milosevic, who was one of the most senior military commanders of the Army of Republika Srpska, the VRS, reaching the apex of his career when on or about August 1994, he was appointed commander of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, the SRK, the corps that surrounded the city of Sarajevo since 1992. This accused was a professional and well-trained career officer and experienced military commander, educated in the well-organised system of the JNA, the Federal Army of Yugoslavia. As part of his training, the accused - like his fellow commanders and staff officers - knew his obligations under the Geneva Conventions and the laws of war. Like few others, however, the accused was intimately familiar, not only with the war in Bosnia, but specifically with the siege of Sarajevo. During the first months of the siege in 1992, the accused became the commander of one of the brigades included in the SRK that surrounded Sarajevo. Already then, he worked closely with General Ratko Mladic, the overall commander of the VRS, who later became his direct superior. Then in July of 1993, the accused became Chief of Staff to the then-SRK commander, General Galic. A little more than a year later in August of 1994, the accused succeeded General Galic, and himself became commander of the SRK. Given this record, the accused could have been under no illusions about the type of campaign that he inherited when he took command of the SRK in August of 1994. The accused remained the commander of the besieging forces of Sarajevo from about 10 August 1994 until November 1995, and as stated in the amended indictment, Your Honours, the accused was both the de jure and de facto commander of the professional force of some 18.000 soldiers and officers, other affiliated VRS units operating in the Sarajevo theatre, and a substantial weapons arsenal. For over 15 months, the accused deployed this force of soldiers and military weaponry to conduct a deliberate campaign of attacks against civilians in the city of Sarajevo and its immediate surroundings, some 350.000 people, designed to spread terror to the population and resulting in the deaths of hundreds of civilians and the maiming of thousands more. This he also did with the knowledge and experience gained in the different positions occupied by him from 1992 onwards in Sarajevo. Let me begin by very briefly putting the events described in the amended indictment into the proper historical context in the war of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This war had its origins in the disintegration of a state in 1991, Yugoslavia, and the emergence of a new state, Bosnia and Herzegovina. Both the Bosnian Serbs and Croats made it clear that they would have recourse to armed conflict rather than accept minority status in a Muslim-dominated state. Following a referendum held in February of 1992, sponsored by the Bosnian Muslims with some support from the Bosnian Croats but boycotted by the Bosnian Serbs, Bosnia and Herzegovina declared its independence in March of 1992. In anticipation of this outcome, on the 9th of January, 1992, the Bosnian Serb political leadership proclaimed a Serbian republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which later became known as Republika Srpska. Hostilities escalated between the factions assigned to these groups, and armed conflict broke out after the European Community recognised Bosnia and Herzegovina as a sovereign state on the 7th of April, 1992. On or about that date, the city of Sarajevo was heavily bombarded by artillery, tanks, and mortar of the JNA -- mortars of the JNA deployed in locations overlooking or in the range of the city. On the 2nd of May, 1992, a major JNA attack on the centre of Sarajevo occurred, thereafter the town was continually exposed to heavy shelling and sniping activity. On the 12th of May, 1992, the Assembly of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Banja Luka considered a plan to ensure that Sarajevo became the political capital of the republic and adopted strategic objectives, one of them being the division of Sarajevo into Serb and Muslim parts. It was understood that Sarajevo must be divided or razed to the ground. At the same meeting, the Assembly created the VRS, designating General Ratko Mladic chief of its General Staff. The nucleus of the VRS was constituted from the 2nd Military District of the JNA which withdrew from Bosnia-Herzegovina shortly thereafter, on or about the 20th of May, 1992. As an offspring of the JNA, one of the most professional armies in eastern Europe, the VRS was able to rely, to a very large extent, upon JNA resources and experiences. Indeed, the VRS took over JNA doctrine and regulations almost verbatim. On the 22nd of May, 1992, Bosnia and Herzegovina was admitted as a member state of the United Nations. The Security Council called for the withdrawal of foreign forces, including the JNA, from its territory. That same day, General Mladic ordered the formation of the SRK, one of the five constituent corps of the VRS. The SRK was formed mainly from elements and materiel of the former JNA 4th Corps that had previously been garrisoned and deployed in and around Sarajevo. The accused, as we know, took over the SRK in August of 1994. Let me focus now on what happened in Sarajevo and let me begin by providing just a little bit of background information about the city itself. We have provided Your Honours with a map book, a number of maps, that we will be using with various witnesses during the trial. As you know, Sarajevo is Bosnia and Herzegovina's capital city and its largest city, and it epitomised the republic's diversity. The city is dominated by steep surrounding mountain slopes. To the east, the Bascarsija area, difficult to pronounce, there is a dense city centre making up a residential and commercial old town which spreads up the adjacent hill-sides, while the new municipalities with commercial development and extensive residential accommodation are on the more open ground to the west of the city. By 1990, the city consisted of ten municipalities, six of which were genuinely urban communities that had either been part of the city for centuries or had been urbanised during the 20th century. Four others had been made part of the city in 1977 but were peripheral to the urban core, but were gradually undergoing urbanisation but nonetheless large tracts of rural, mountainous terrain on the city's periphery. Sarajevo was largely integrated residentially and home to a flourishing communal life, to use the socialist-era term for the phenomenon that later became more widely known as multi-ethnic life. Certainly by 1990, the urbanised centre had become ethnically mixed and many Sarajevans lived in high-rise apartment buildings without regard to national identity. Members of various ethnicities mingled freely in everyday affairs, honoured one other with mutual visits on appropriate holidays. Sarajevo's communal life was highlighted by their shared pride in hosting the 14th Olympic winter games in 1984. A 1991 census indicated that the city and immediate surroundings had a population of some 525.988, with an ethnic composition of 49.3 per cent Muslim, 29.9 per cent Serb, 6.6 per cent Croat, 10.7 describing themselves as Yugoslav, and 3.5 per cent other groups. Sarajevo accounted for 11 per cent of the population of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In sum, Your Honours, from every Sarajevan who will testify before you in the next few months, you will here that before 1992, Sarajevo was a blooming multi-ethnic community and a cultural and economic centre in the former Yugoslavia. Sarajevo is a great city with a rich history going back for nearly 2.000 years. It has always proudly displayed its tolerance and respect for its inhabitants. Your Honours, the mentioned topographical characteristics of the city made Sarajevo extremely vulnerable to the SRK military as by April and May 1992, it had positioned its forces on the high ground encircling the valley, giving it a significant advantage over the defending forces in Sarajevo, the Bosnian Army, which I will refer to as the ABiH. Thought the siege -- throughout the siege, Sarajevo remained vulnerable to bombardment from the hills north and south. I already mentioned the start of the shelling and sniping campaign as of April 1992. The objective of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in relation to Sarajevo was clear by May 1992, according to the stated objective of division or destruction. This objective was repeated and was acted upon. The minister of health of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina stated as follows: "I am for the destruction of the Kosevo hospital so that the enemy has nowhere to go for medical help." The Prosecution will demonstrate that such words were not empty words. Your Honours, to quote from the report of Prosecution expert Robert Donia: "The Bosnian Serb leaders used their military and geographic advantages to shell Sarajevo periodically, to damage and destroy its cultural and religious monuments, and to deprive its civilian population of food, water, electricity, gas, and transportation. The city's diminished population became dependent on international humanitarian aid to sustain life. Widespread starvation was averted owing to the efforts of UNPROFOR and the ingenuity of Sarajevo's defenders." For the next three and a half years, the two opposing armies fought to a position of stalemate, and apart from a few flare-ups the confrontation lines became static, reflect the protracted stranglehold of the SRK. Although the ABiH in Sarajevo had four times as many troops as the SRK, with some 75.000 soldiers defending the city, the SRK had a weapons advantage and by early 1993 had surrounded the city with mortars, tanks, howitzers, anti-aircraft guns, and other heavy weapons. The accused commanded some seven infantry brigades, a military police battalion, a light artillery regiment, an anti-tank battalion, in addition to the several corps command departments that he controlled. The Bosnian government forces defending Sarajevo --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down for the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I apologise. I will slow down. The Bosnian government forces defending Sarajevo, namely the ABiH 1st Corps commanded by General Vahid Karevelic, was also organised into brigades which were located throughout the city of Sarajevo. The Prosecution will bring ample evidence showing that the SRK employed trained snipers or sharpshooters within their ranks who targeted civilians in Sarajevo from long distances. As a clear example of the employment of snipers within the SRK, the Prosecution will offer into evidence an order signed by the accused on the 19th of January, 1995, wherein he organised the transport of instructors or trainers were snipers to be transported to military barracks in Jahorina so that they could commence their work. Just preceding that order, on the 15th of January, 1995, the commander of the 3rd Sarajevo Infantry Brigade sent a request to the accused for sniping training of their soldiers. The Prosecution points out that for purposes of this case "sniper," the term "sniper," does not just refer to a person with a rifle or direct-fire weapon with an optical sight, rather that sniping is the direct targeting of individuals at a distance from a concealed or partially concealed position by a small- calibre weapon, such as a rifle or a machine-gun; in other words, from single- and multiple-shot weapons. In addition, by April 1995, the SRK introduced into its arsenal weapons known as modified air-bombs, that - as will be discussed later - possessed great destructive power but which were unguidable and therefore completely inaccurate. They added another dimension to the already existing state of terror to which the civilian population of Sarajevo had been reduced. The campaign to inflict terror and fear on the civilian population of Sarajevo was orchestrated by the accused through both shelling and sniping simultaneously. Civilians riding on trams in downtown Sarajevo were just as much at risk of death and injury from sniping or other small arms fire as the civilians who lived in the Sarajevan suburb of Hrasnica south-west of the city were from modified air-bombs. The twin campaign of shelling and sniping was pervasive and enveloped the whole city. Some areas, due to their topographical and geographical disadvantage, were more prone to attacks than others, such as the residential settlement of Sredenik to the north-east of the city, which was a prime target from the infamous snipers at their nest at sharpstone. The timing of the shelling and sniping could not be predicted, only that a week would not go by without civilians being shelled or sniped at. Some periods were more intense than others, such as the barrage of modified air-bomb attacks in the summer of 1995. But generally, and as the Prosecution intends to prove with the illustrative incidents detailed in the two schedules of sniping and shelling appended to the amended indictment, the campaign of shelling and sniping continued throughout the tenure of the command of the accused. Even when NATO strikes were called in and the international community enforced a weapons exclusion zone in September of 1995, the Prosecution will bring witness and documentary evidence to show that the attacks continued. It is thus important to stress, Your Honours, that this case is not about legitimate military actions against military targets; it's about targeting civilians through direct, indiscriminate, and disproportionate fire. The period of the amended indictment is co-extensive with the period during which the accused was the commander of the SRK. And during that period, the SRK did launch attacks against legitimate military objectives within the environs of Sarajevo. These attacks do not, however, form any part of the charges against the accused, even where such attacks may have resulted in proportionate or incidental civilian casualties or fear. What the accused is charged with, however, is the campaign he led against the civilian population of Sarajevo. In doing that, Your Honours, the accused violated one of the key principles of international humanitarian law, the principle of distinction. Every military commander has the duty to make a distinction between military targets and civilian targets -- or, in other words, to distinguish between soldiers and legitimate military objectives, such as weaponry or headquarters on the one side, and civilians and civilian objects, such as apartment houses, on the other. As commander in 1994 and 1995, the accused, General Milosevic, knew this basic and crucial tenet of international humanitarian law. What are indiscriminate attacks, Your Honours? These are aimless attacks in the sense that shells were fired into residential areas without directing them at any particular targets at all and without regard to the high possibility of excessive civilian casualties. Were civilians targeted? Yes. You will see at the end of this opening a few graphic images of Sarajevo with civilians being exposed to sniping fire. Victims will testify as to their own experiences. In addition, the seige of Sarajevo was witnessed by many international military and civilian observers, some of who will appear shortly before Your Honours to tell exactly what they witnessed. For these officers, the deliberateness of the terror inflicted on Sarajevo was palpable. Was it possible that the weaponry was inaccurate and the gunners made mistakes? The Prosecution will present expert and fact witness evidence to prove that although mortars are typically indirect-fire weapons, the SRK gunners were able to deploy them to such an accurate standard that a target could be hit at first attempt. A mortar shell is specifically designed to kill and maim people. The SRK mortars encircling Sarajevo on the high ground remained in the same positions throughout the conflict, their base plates were dug-in, and so targets had been recorded. By the time the accused took command, such targets could be engaged with a high degree of accuracy. Of course, the issue of accuracy is even less applicable to modified air-bombs, as will be shown during the trial with expert and fact witnesses. These weapons were so inaccurate and unguidable that their use in an urban environment, such as Sarajevo, was, the Prosecution says, per se illegal, as the risk of excessive civilian casualties was so high. A clear indication of the fact that the SRK engaged civilian targets rather than legitimate military ones will be proved by Prosecution evidence showing that known military installations of the defence of Sarajevo were left untouched. For instance, the headquarters of the ABiH 1st Corps, the military opponent of the SRK, was only hit once during the entire conflict. The headquarters' location was well-known to anybody in the Sarajevo war theatre. In sum, the purpose of the SRK's military campaign was not primarily to hit military targets. The civilians were the main targets in Sarajevo, and they were targeted because the SRK was carrying out psychological warfare on civilians to force a capitulation of the enemy. One of the many experienced international military witnesses who was in Sarajevo in the summer of 1995, Mr. Fortin, and who will appear before you shortly will testify that sniping was a very efficient military tactic in warfare. However, he thought that it was used in Sarajevo more as a terror tactic. In sum, why would a military force fire shells into a predominantly residential area of Sarajevo with complete abandon as to where the shells would land and with complete disregard as to whether civilians were killed or injured as a result? The reason is that it did not matter what was hit. The primary purpose of the attack was to terrify the civilian population, and in that objective the SRK succeeded. Taking up this thought, Your Honours, I would like to devote the next few minutes - and it's the last part of my part of this opening statement - to the victims. What was daily life like in Sarajevo under Dragomir Milosevic's tenure as the commander of the SRK? Day-to-day activities continued to be life-and-death situations. Throughout the icy winters of the war, Sarajevans had to make the daily choice between freezing in their homes from the cold or risking their lives to venture out to collect firewood or water. Moving through the city in search of a loaf of bread was a death-defying act. As family members headed out into the besieged Sarajevo streets for day-to-day supplies, it was always a question whether they would return. The Prosecution will present evidence from the survivors of the Markale Market massacre of 28th August 1995, which is scheduled incident number 23, the second time a civilian marketplace was shelled by the SRK, the first time being on 5th February, 1994, under the commander of General Galic. At the end of today's opening, you will watch footage and hear witnesses describe the scene of carnage, destruction, panic, and terror. The Prosecution will present testimony from several tram drivers who took daily risks to bring Sarajevo civilians in and around -- in and out of the centre of the city. The bend in the tracks in front of the Holiday Inn where the tram slows down was a notorious target of SRK snipers under the command of the accused. The Prosecution will bring -- will bring evidence of scores of civilian victims of tram shootings and shellings. At the end of today's presentation, to illustrate, Your Honours will see a short video footage about attacks at trams. The Prosecution will also present the testimony of several witnesses who fell victim to the modified air-bombs. They will describe the physical horrors of the devastation caused by these weapons, including the massive scale of the damage. You will hear of one incident where a modified air-bomb severely damaged 11 houses, causing injury and death to civilians within that radius, and another incident where one modified air- bomb completely destroyed three floors of a building, causing damage also to other buildings in the vicinity. Again, in this case, civilian casualties were extensive. You will also watch civilians grouped at intersections, summoning up the courage to run for their lives across an opening which exposed them as targets in the SRK line of fire. When some fell victim, others ran across to bring the injured to safety. When civilians, including the elderly, children, and women, were shot by SRK snipers or shelled by SRK forces, often rescue workers or local authorities could not reach them to bring them to safety and medical treatment because the sniping and shelling continued, targeting the same people who had already been hit as well as their rescuers. The Prosecution will present witness testimony and show footage of such rescue attempts; the injured victims of SRK sniping and their rescuers both under attack by SRK forces under the command of the accused. Those who made it to the hospital, in spite of the ongoing sniping and shelling, received whatever treatment could be given. The floors of the hospital were frequently lined with injured civilians. Even when victims were buried, loved ones risked their lives, standing at the graves in line of sight of SRK snipers. Civilians were killed while attending funerals. Your Honours, not only the victims, the civilians of Sarajevo will come and testify about the terror they experienced on a daily basis. In support of and to corroborate the account of the local witnesses, you will hear the testimony and be presented with reports from a number of members of the international community. I'll quote just one report dated the 8th of July, 1995, drafted by a witness who is going to be called in this case, David Harland, in which he says the following: "Despite the reduction in military activity around the city, the harassment of the civilian population continues almost unabated. Sniping and mortaring are still at a reasonably high level. This seems to have no particular military value but contributes to a general atmosphere of terror in the city. Almost no civilians now use the city's main east-west thoroughfare 'sniper alley,' so much so that snipers who used to work that area now seem to have relocated." Your Honours, that concludes my part of the opening statement. I will now turn to Mr. Waespi who will talk to Your Honours about -- more specifically about the accused and about the indictment in this case. I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting. Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours. Born in Serbia in 1942, Dragomir Milosevic, the accused, was a competent commanding and staff officer at all times and in all functions during his considerable career in the JNA and the VRS. His progress on his career path indicates that his superiors valued his professional skills and leadership qualities. As stated earlier, he had been an officer in the JNA before the armed conflict, having served as a regimental Chief of Staff and then brigade Chief of Staff of the 49th Motorised Brigade at Lukavica of the 4th Corps, 2nd Military District. At least from September 1990, he was the commander of the 216th Mountain Brigade, again within the 4th Corps, located in Han Pijesak. With the creation of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps in May 1992, the 216th Mountain Brigade was renamed the 1st Romanija Infantry Brigade and the accused remained the commander of this brigade until the beginning of 1993. The accused was later - as we already heard - Chief of Staff of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps from at least 4th of July, 1993, until 10th August, 1994, when he became the commander of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. For his services, the accused, in the same year he took over command of the SRK, was awarded with the star of Karadjordjevic, the 1st Order. Your Honours, you will hear testimony that the accused was a proper, professional, and brave officer. Witnesses will describe the accused as a hands-on commander, who often visited his troops in the field to learn more about the tactical situation and to boost morale. For this, the accused was respected by his soldiers and his orders were followed throughout the ranks. Sarajevo's untold horrors were not new to Dragomir Milosevic when he took over his position as the corps commander in August 1994. As mentioned, the accused had not only been the commander of a brigade of the SRK, with elements, Your Honours, located conveniently in Grbavica, incidentally a notorious source of SRK fire during the siege, in early summer 1992 when the first shells were launched on to Sarajevo. Even more significantly, in July 1993, the accused became the Chief of Staff to the then-SRK commander, General Galic. Of course, Your Honours, the accused is not charged with crimes that were committed outside the timeframe of this indictment and before he took over command of the SRK. However, Your Honours, it's the Prosecution's case that in particular, the fact that the accused occupied the key role as a corps Chief of Staff over the extended period of time of over a year, during which horrible crimes were committed, is relevant in as much as from day one of his tenure as corps commander he was put, to the very least, on notice of the terror campaign that was led by his predecessor. As the number two in the SRK structure, and second only to the commander, as General Galic's right-hand man, the accused was privy to information, including day-to-day details of SRK movements and activities. His signature appears on daily combat reports as early as 6th July 1993, in this case he signed as deputy SRK commander. Your Honours, the moment the accused assumed command of the SRK by virtue of the past positions he had, he was thoroughly apprised of the numerous military issues relating to the Sarajevo theatre. In particular, he knew of any significant ABiH 1st Corps locations, such as headquarters, and therefore potential military targets. He knew in full detail the inventory of SRK weaponry, his own assets; where the heavy weapons were located; and how and when to acquire more weaponry. He was clearly supremely knowledgeable, as was his job, of the various brigade and battalion locations within his corps. He knew of their commanders and regularly met with them. The accused was also familiar with the location of the confrontation lines and corps logistical issues and the lines and practice of reporting up and down the chain of command. In short, Your Honours, the accused's previous positions within the SRK rendered him more than capable of taking steps to deviate from the policy of shelling and sniping of civilians so as to spread terror if he so wanted, but as the evidence will show, Your Honours, he did not; rather, he perpetuated it. As commander of the corps, the SRK, the accused performed - and we will show you ample evidence of that - command and control functions through an arrangement of personnel, equipment, communications, facilities, and procedures by way of planning, directing, coordinating, and controlling forces under his command. He had full command over the SRK and other subordinated units. The notion of full command covered all aspects of military operations and administration. In the context of his operational command, he could assign tasks to subordinate commanders, deploy units, and retain or delegate operational or tactical control as he felt necessary. And I will show you an example later today. By regulating the process of combat reporting, the accused addressed an essential element of the commander's ability to exercise operational command: Awareness of the tactical and operational situation. As a corps commander, the accused had all prerogatives, de jure and de facto, to exercise his authority to establish and maintain a level of discipline foreseen for a professional army. How does the Prosecution intend to prove its case, Your Honours? The Prosecution will seek to prove its case bearing in mind several factors, all of which have been taken into account in the development of the Prosecution's case thus far. First of all, the charges, Your Honours. The Prosecution has charged the accused with a campaign of shelling and sniping, the primary purpose of which was to spread terror among the civilian population. The nature of these charges, crimes against humanity, and violation of the laws or customs of war, requires the Prosecution to prove this to the Court beyond a reasonable doubt, not only the specific elements of each crime, but also the so-called common elements of war crimes and crime against humanity. Proving its case requires admitting both crime base evidence, evidence of the mass scale of these crimes, and finally the link directly to the accused, proving his individual criminal responsibility for the crimes he's charged with. As in the Galic case, the common elements of the crimes charged, the campaign, will be partially proven through the use of illustrative sniping and shelling incidents, as outlined in the two schedules of the indictment. Thus, the Prosecution case will necessarily include evidence to prove each of our scheduled sniping and shelling incidents beyond a reasonable doubt, but will also include pattern and overview evidence of the terror campaign wrought by Dragomir Milosevic and his SRK subordinates against the civilian population of Sarajevo, as well as evidence of the criminal role of the accused in carrying out the campaign. A second factor, Your Honours, of which the Prosecution is also aware is the need to streamline our cases to ensure a speedy trial, which protects the rights of the accused. Thirdly, the Prosecution is keenly aware that evidence of the suffering of civilians from the same type of criminal activity in Sarajevo has been presented in other cases before this Tribunal, and that some of the same witnesses who have testified in prior cases would also provide evidence of the crimes charged in the indictment against the accused, Dragomir Milosevic. Significantly, the Prosecution notes that it is always a difficult and traumatic endeavour for victims of crimes to come and testify live, so the Prosecution has borne this in mind when deciding on its witnesses. The Prosecution has thus sought to balance all these factors in determining its methodology for proving this case. To address the individual crime-base evidence, the Prosecution will lead evidence of crime-base witnesses, victims, eye-witnesses, local investigators, and international personnel present at particular sniping or shelling incidents. However, Mr. President and Your Honours, in doing so, the Prosecution will seem to apply the mechanisms allowed by the Rules and practice of this Court to reduce the necessary court time. The Prosecution will thus be seeking to admit most of the evidence of crime base witnesses pursuant to Rule 92 bis and ter with the witnesses, if Your Honours so order, present in court to confirm their prior statements and to be cross- examined. As this Court is aware, the Prosecution has already reduced the number of shelled incidents from 23 -- shelling incidents down to 15, and the number of illustrative sniping incidents from 20 down to 12, with the ultimate aim of streamlining the case and reducing the number of courtroom hours needed by the Prosecution by a third of the original estimate. These remaining shelled incidents will be proven not only through witness testimony but also through video footage, UN reports, and reports of other international organisations, photographs, hospital records, and criminal investigation reports. Some witnesses, Your Honours, have particular circumstances, like age or health issues, which may require the use of videolink to enable them to testify; this will not, however, preclude the Prosecution from seeking to limit the length of required court time for their testimonies through the use of Rule 92 ter and it will ensure they are available for cross-examination by the Defence. Pattern evidence of the campaign, Your Honours, to satisfy the common elements of the crimes charged, will be presented by the Prosecution through the testimony of international personnel, primarily former UN military observers and former officers of UNPROFOR, journalists, local police, investigators, and expert witnesses. All of them, Your Honours, will provide evidence beyond the limited number of scheduled incidents and talk about other unscheduled examples of the many incidents of attacks against the civilian population during the period of the amended indictment. Finally, and most importantly, the Prosecution will bring evidence of the individual criminal responsibility of the accused. Witnesses who will testify to the role of the accused in carrying out the terror campaign of sniping and shelling will include individuals who worked closely with the accused in conducting the campaign, witnesses who were present at times when action was taken in pursuit of the policy of the campaign, and also international personnel, including high-level UN officials who protested directly to the accused, either in writing or in person. Again, Your Honours, the Prosecution will be seeking to admit much of this evidence pursuant to Rule 92 ter, to ensure presentation of its evidence in as efficient as possible a manner. Before I turn to the specific counts of the indictment, Mr. President and Your Honours, I would like to make you a bit more familiar with the layout of the city as it relates to the charged, selected scheduled incidents. May I ask you, Mr. President, Your Honours, to go to that picture book my colleague, Alex Whiting, talked about which had been facilitated to you yesterday, the same pictures and photos and charts will be available on your computer screen as well. The first map you see on the screen, Your Honours - and it's actually map number 2 in your booklet - shows you what Mr. Whiting talked about, the layout of the city and the municipalities. Old town in the middle, other settlements outside, notably Pale to the east. The second map, Your Honours, relates to the military activity of the accused. You have heard from Mr. Whiting about the VRS. The VRS had at that time, in 1995, six corps. One of the corps, the SRK, Sarajevo Romanija Corps, was led by the accused, and you can see on this map - and it's map 4 in your bundle - you can see the outline of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, and I have to say and there will be witnesses who can be more accurate if required. The next map, Your Honours, and that's number 6 in your bundle, and again it does appear on your computer screen as well, is by way of example a contemporaneous map from the ABiH, the 1st Corps, it's called a working map of the staff of this 1st Corps. And you will hear from its commander, Mr. Karevelic, who can explain the features on this map. It shows, not very easily visible, the layout of the city, the way the AbiH, in broad sense, had its own brigades allocated inside the city, and it shows the confrontation lines as well. What I want to do with this map, Your Honours, just very briefly show you a few of the key locations witnesses as early as next Monday will talk about. Your Honours might be familiar with many of them because of your previous experience in Sarajevo-related cases. Nevertheless, here are the features. Your Honours, how does the Prosecution intend to present our incidents, the shelling and sniping incidents? Let me first talk about sniping as it relates to Counts 2 and 4 of the amended indictment. The nature of the individual crimes which constitute the crime base for the indictment are such that they are difficult to convey into a courtroom. In the case of sniping, Your Honours, they involve persons being shot in the open. In circumstances where the killer is secluded, in the case of shelling, the use of indirect fire means that those who were present at the place where the shell landed generally did not see where the shell emanated from. In order to better assist the Trial Chamber, the Prosecution has prepared a video of each of the shelling and sniping incidents. In relation to the number -- numbered shelling and sniping incidents, if the victim survived and is available to give evidence, the victim was videoed at the scene, pointing out precisely where they were at the time they were hit by the bullet. The exercise was undertaken in summer 2006. If, however, Your Honours the victim was fatally wounded, an eye- witness to the incident appears on the video, pointing out to the best of their recollection where the victim was at precisely the moment that they were shot. A tripod was erected at the exact location of the victim's position he or she was shot, and the camera lens fixed at the height approximately the height of the point of entry on the body of the victim of the bullet. A professional photographer then took photographs depicting a 360-degree view from that position, the position where the bullet entered the body of the victim. These photographs were later joined up so that a continuous 360- degree image can be made available to the Trial Chamber. Defence counsel was invited to attend the filming of some of these incidents in the summer. The scheduled shelling incidents were videoed in a similar fashion. I will take you now, Your Honours, to one sample incident using this technology and the incident is scheduled incident number 5. The schedule for that incident reads as stated in the First Schedule to the amended indictment. "18 November 1994. Dzenana Sokolovic, a woman aged 31 years, and her son Nermin Divovic, a boy aged 7 years, were fired on while walking in Zmaj od Bosne. Ms. Sokolovic was wounded with a bullet in the abdomen. The bullet passed through her and hit her son in the head, killing him. They had been walking home from Hrasno, where they had gone to collect firewood the previous day." Dzenana and her children hardly moved from her home between 1992 and 1995, she will tell the Court during her testimony. They were afraid to even open their front door due to the instant sniping and shelling which targeted the civilian population. Dzenana did all she could to protect her family from these constant attacks, but in the end her worst nightmare came true. Dzenana and her children had hardly anything to eat and lived in constant fear. They lived in anticipation of being attacked any time of the day. On the 18th of November, 1994, at approximately 11.00 in the morning, Dzenana emerged from her house to collect firewood. It was a time of a cease-fire, and the Sokolovic family urgently needed wood to provide them with heat in the cold November weather. Dzenana and her children went to the mother-in-law's house to collect firewood. As they returned with a bundle of wood, Dzenana's son was to her left and her daughter just behind them. Suddenly, the three came under fire from SRK forces. Dzenana heard shots, saw the other civilians around her falling to the ground, and then felt a pain, a sharp pain in her abdomen. She also noticed her son fall to the ground. UNPROFOR personnel were nearby, and as they attempted to rescue Dzenana and her children, they all came under continuous SRK sniper fire. Dzenana was finally rushed to the hospital, where she underwent surgery. Only later when she awoke did she learn that her son had died on the spot; the bullet had gone through her stomach, her own stomach, and into her son's head. Dzenana's son Nermin was buried on the 21st of November, 1994, whilst Dzenana was still in hospital. She was unable to attend his funeral. Your Honours, I would like to demonstrate to you, using this example, how the Prosecution intends to present this incident to you in this trial. Yes, I think you have seen the point, Mr. President and Your Honours, that's a way the Prosecution the present shelling -- sniping evidence in relation to each single piece of -- incident we want to prove. Let me continue with shelling, Mr. President and Your Honours. At this point, the Prosecution underscores that the shelling component is part of the overall campaign of attacks against civilians, along with sniping, the primary purpose of which was to spread terror among the civilian population. It is also not confined to the illustrative incidents set forth in the Second Schedule of the indictment, but it will also be evidenced by more general, overview evidence of deliberate, indiscriminate, and disproportionate attacks against civilians. The Prosecution will present detailed evidence relating to 15 shelling incidents which are illustrative of the campaign. These incidents will demonstrate that the location and timing of the shelling attacks were launched in such places as to predictably cause extensive civilian casualties. Or, in the case of indiscriminate fire, with complete disregard to the possibility of excessive civilian casualties, rendering these actions the deliberate targeting of civilians. The illustrative incidents show that the campaign of shelling was conducted during business hours where public markets were located on a water distribution point provided for the civilians to access a source so limited due to ongoing blockade and bombardment by the accused's subordinates of the SRK, on a medical facility, a television tower where local and foreign journalists worked, and on exclusively residential areas within the city. Civilians of both sexes, of all ages, including children and the elderly, of all ethnicities, and of all professions, were the target. Further, the Prosecution will present evidence that for each of these incidents there was no military target in the area or military activity taking place at the time of the shelling. There was also no military necessity. No one and nowhere were immune from artillery and mortar attacks in Sarajevo during the indictment period. No area could be presumed safe for the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, I think this may be a convenient time to take a break for 20 minutes. We'll adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may continue, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. No example of the sheer terror and destruction visited upon the civilians of Sarajevo by the firing and exploding of mortar bombs is more graphic than the firing incident on the marketplace on 28th August 1995. The Prosecution will show that on that bright summer's day, SRK fired a 120-millimetre mortar bomb on a crowded, bustling market close to noon in broad daylight, killing 43 civilians and injuring 75 more. The site of the massacre was just opposite to a similar heinous mortar attack by the SRK that occurred at the outdoor Markale Market on 5th February 1994. Markale II, as it became to be infamously known, was no less terrifying and no less destructive as you will see from a video footage which I will show to you at the end of today's opening address. The Prosecution, Your Honours, will call eyewitnesses to testify about the human carnage and destruction depicted so graphically on this video clip. It will also present evidence that will show that the time -- that at that time, there was no military target in the vicinity of the marketplace and that the preponderance of those injured and killed were civilians. It's worth noting that this incident sent shockwaves around the world, and governments and the United Nations were united in their swift condemnation of the incident and the extensive human casualties caused. In fact, once the investigations established that the SRK had fired the killing round, this finally tipped the scales with NATO seeking permission to commence air-strikes on VRS military positions in Pale and elsewhere. Your Honours, the Prosecution will bring expert and fact witness evidence that will prove beyond a reasonable doubt that subordinates of the accused fired this 120-millimetre mortar from the mountain of Trebevic situated towards the south of the city. United Nations military observers and local police inspectors will provide details of their in-depth crater investigations, establishing the probable angle of descent and direction of fire, and crucially an UNMO, United Nations military observer, will be called to testify that while on observation along the established direction of the mortar in ABiH-held territory, he did not hear the firing of a 120- millimetre mortar at the relevant time from the area, a firing sound he would have heard if it had been fired from within ABiH territory. This was, Your Honours, a deliberate attack perpetrated by SRK members as part of a campaign of terror orchestrated by the accused. As if the mortar and artillery attacks against civilians were not sufficiently destructive and terrorising, in April 1995, well into the tenure of the accused's command and after a succession of deadly mortar and other artillery attacks in the latter part of 1994, the SRK, on the orders and organisation of the accused, started to deploy and launch a more sinister weapon called modified air-bomb. These weapons were of great destructive powers, Your Honours. They killed numerous civilians and caused extensive damage to buildings, such as houses and apartments. Their deployment clearly perpetuated and even increased the terrorisation of the civilian population of Sarajevo. Prosecution will present expert and fact witnesses -- witness evidence from both the SRK and ABiH or Bosnian police that will demonstrate that this makeshift weapon was incapable of being guided, as it was a projectile designed to be dropped from an aeroplane, but instead, on most occasions, fired from the back of a truck with rockets strapped on it. A member of the accused's corps command, corps staff, will give evidence of the inaccuracy, the inherent inaccuracy, of these modified air-bombs. Such was the inability to guide the modified air-bombs at all. The Prosecution's case is that even if the intention was to direct them at legitimate military targets, this could not be done and thus the possibility of extensive civilian casualties was so excessive in an urban environment such as Sarajevo, that their use at all, regardless of the intended target, was contrary to international humanitarian law and illegal, as the principle of distinction could not have been applied. The Prosecution will present evidence from ABiH personnel, experts, and SRK personnel that only the SRK possessed and used these modified air-bombs in the city of Sarajevo. In this regard, it is the Prosecution's case then -- that whenever a modified air-bomb was used and exploded within the city or in areas, such as Hrasnica, a residential settlement on the outskirts of the city, south-west, the firing area of origin was always SRK territory under the effective control of the accused, and that their use was either known or - as I will show in a moment - directly ordered by the accused. In this regard, the Prosecution will bring expert evidence showing that whenever these modified air-bombs were fired, they made a huge sound that could easily be picked up. If these bombs had been fired from within the ABiH front lines, it could not have been undertaken without triggering a response from the scores of United Nations observers and other internationals within the city. There is no evidence, Your Honours, that this was the case. The accused's shelling campaign with these unguided, modified air-bombs commenced in earnest in April 1994 [sic] and continued with high intensity and frequency throughout the summer months of May, June, July 1995. During that narrow period, as the illustrative allegations in the amended indictment show, the SRK launched modified air-bombs that on at least 13 occasions caused civilian casualties and building damage. From the 13 incidents appended to the amended indictment, some 104 casualties were caused by the explosion of modified air-bombs, with thousands more terrorised. The Prosecution will bring witness and contemporaneous documentary evidence that show beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused knew that artillery, mortar fire, and modified air-bombs that could not be guided were being deployed against civilian targets. Senior United Nations military commanders and civilian officials will give evidence of how they relayed to the accused in written form and verbally, Your Honours, unequivocal protest of the use of air-bombs and shelling generally against civilian targets. A little later on, Your Honours, I will show you just one such protest when UNPROFOR Colonel Robert Meille wrote to the accused on the 1st of July, 1995, just after an SRK attack on the TV building that killed one person and injured 28 persons. Your Honours, just to note that this incident, this attack on the TV tower, is scheduled incident number 15 in our amended indictment. In this letter, Mr. President, Your Honours, Colonel Meille also vehemently protested over a subsequent attack by mortar rounds on the residential areas of Alapasino Polje and an attack on the PTT building which was, as I told you earlier, the headquarters of UNPROFOR, Sector Sarajevo. In this protest, Colonel Meille reminds the accused and his subordinates to: "Moral and legal obligations to adhere to the Geneva Conventions ..." specifically referring to Article 85 of the Protocol I of the Geneva Conventions. In fact, the accused already knew what he was told about by Colonel Meille. His knowledge came from his own troops, as is evidenced in a, and I quote the title, "Report on the Situation at the Front," drafted by the accused and dated 30th June, 1995, when the accused commends the heroism of his units, specifically mentioning that in one such incident on the 28th of June, 1995, his artillery units hit the BiH TV building. Your Honours, this is a good example of actual knowledge of the accused of activities of his subordinate troops, as would be expected from a corps commander. The Prosecution will be introducing this document in due course. The Prosecution will also bring evidence that the accused himself ordered the possession, deployment, and indeed launching of modified air- bombs. These heavy weapons were controlled at the higher levels, and it's inconceivable that one could be launched without it being either ordered by the accused, the SRK command, or without the knowledge -- or without the knowledge of the accused. In one such glaring example, the accused orders the firing of a modified air-bomb from Ilidza into Hrasnica on 6th April 1995. This is, again, one of the only four documents I will be showing you in a moment. True enough, Your Honours, on the following day, 7th April, 1995, a day after the order of the accused, indeed a modified air-bomb was fired on Hrasnica residential neighbourhood, killing one person and injuring three, as well as causing severe damage to the dwellings. Your Honours, this is scheduled shelling incident number 6, as charged in the amended indictment, and you will hear victims' testimony about that during the course of this trial. A crime, Your Honours, directly ordered by the accused, the SRK corps commander. The Prosecution alleges that the lethal bomb was fired from SRK-controlled area of Ilidza, the area of responsibility of the brigade to which the accused had sent the order the day before. Your Honours, I would just like to show you four documents - I intended five but we will skip one - four documents to see the types of evidence the Prosecution intends to show during the trial in terms of documents. All these documents will be introduced by various means, live witnesses or perhaps from the bar table as self-propelled documents, as they are called sometimes. Let me go to the first document, Mr. President, Your Honours, the 65 ter number is 1969, and it's a document of 12th August 1994, authored by the accused. You can see on your screen first the B/C/S original version of the document, two-page document, but I'll lead you through a few points of the English translation. Mr. President, Your Honours, this is the third day the accused was in command of the corps, and he issues this order of considerable relevancy to this case. The accused brings selected units of his corps to full combat readiness. The reason, Your Honours, is obvious, as you see in paragraph 1 of the order: Any attacks from the encircled ABiH units had to be prevented. The first important feature of this order for you to note is - still in paragraph 1 - the fact that the accused, as the overall responsible commander of the Bosnian Serb forces around Sarajevo, addresses his order for full combat readiness, not only to all genuine SRK military units on the positions and in the regions of deployment around Sarajevo, but also, and I quote, "MUP units and people under work obligation." This is consistent, Your Honours, with the Prosecution's case, as stated in the amended indictment, that the accused had effective control over all Bosnian Serb forces around Sarajevo. Paragraph 5, Your Honours, further reinforces this point where the accused orders that among SRK units --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Although, Mr. Waespi, just -- I noted that the purpose of ordering full readiness those forces was a preventive one, but you're citing it for another purpose?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: That's fair enough. It just shows that the accused could, in fact --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: -- give orders to these MUP forces for whatever purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The paragraph 5, Mr. President, further reinforces this point, where the accused orders that among SRK units, also the MUP - the police, as you're aware, Your Honours - is to be engaged under the orders of the SRK. Mr. President, that's again the same argument I made before. Incidentally, I invite Your Honours to note what the accused orders his subordinates to do: "To plan forces to block UN units." There are other important features of this document which Your Honours should be aware of, apart from the fact that the document mentions quite a number of units under the accused's overall command. Paragraph 7 illustrates a point made earlier that the SRK command kept their artillery assets on a very tight leash: "Fire to be opened according to the order of the Sarajevo Romanija command post." The order in paragraph 9 also underscores the obvious point when it refers to military doctrine: "Reports on measures undertaken and development of the situation in the mentioned areas are to be made regularly and extraordinarily." In essence, Your Honours, this order shows the way the accused is about to conduct his command for the next 15 months during the period covered by the indictment: A corps commander willing to keep things under firm control from day one. As mentioned, the accused issued this order on his third day in command. Let me skip the anti-sniping agreement. Mr. Harland, who was a participant in the ceremony of signing the document, will be our first witness. He can tell you all about the anti-sniping document. Let me move to the next document, it's 65 ter 2105, 6 November 1994, a document ordered by Mr. Mladic. Perhaps the B/C/S version can be shown first. That's, Your Honour, the original version, and it is a document addressed to the SRK command, corps command of the accused, and carries the heading: "Combat operations in the heavy weapons exclusion zone, order." It reads as follows, and I suggest that Your Honours read it in full because it carries some considerable weight in our submission. I quote -- Mladic says: "I have been informed that the leadership of the Serbian Sarajevo local authorities met with the commander of the SRK in the Vogosca on 5th November 1994, where they adopted a decision to blockade the UNPROFOR, capture the heavy weapons under the UNPROFOR control, and use them to fire at civilian targets in the city of Sarajevo." Mladic then goes on: "Bearing in mind that such decisions could have far-reaching negative effects on the Serbian people and that these combat operations are being planned without my knowledge, I hereby order..." and he orders four points. Mladic, as you know, is the commander of the VRS, the immediate superior of the accused, Dragomir Milosevic. He orders: "1. I forbid all activities aimed at the blockade of UNPROFOR and the seizure of heavy weapons under their control without my specific order and approval. "2. I forbid the planning and carrying out of any offensive combat operation without the approval of the Main Staff of the Republika Srpska army or the implementation of operations planned without the agreement and approval of the Main Staff." And the third point, a significant one, Your Honours: "I forbid firing from large-calibre weapons at civilian targets in Sarajevo without my approval." Third point. And then the fourth paragraph is: "The Sarajevo Romanija Corps commander and his immediate subordinates are personally responsible to me for implementing this order. The SRK commander shall inform his immediate subordinates of this order." Your Honours, this is an amazing document. It not only shows that the SRK command was clearly aware that civilian targets were being hit in their area of responsibility. This document is an admission that the accused, together with local authorities, indeed decided to deliberately target civilians. The Prosecution says that this is a decision made by the accused since it affects his heavy weaponry; it could not have emanated from the local authorities. And the planned attacks on civilians were to be carried out with heavy weaponry stolen from the protection of UNPROFOR, whose task it was to prevent exactly that, the shelling and sniping of civilians. I would like to move on to the next document, Your Honours, this is 65 ter number 2279; it dates 6 April 1995; author, the accused Dragomir Milosevic. And the document is addressed to the Ilidza Infantry Brigade one of the subordinate units of Dragomir Milosevic. I quote from the document: "In order to thwart the enemy and give them a warning so that they are forced to accept this truce, I hereby order: "1. The Ilidza Brigade will immediately prepare a launcher with an aerial bomb and transport the bomb for launching. The most profitable target must be selected in Hrasnica or Sokolovic colony where the greatest casualties and material damage would be inflicted. "Inform me personally of readiness for implementation of this task." That's an order by the corps commander, the accused Dragomir Milosevic. The document, Your Honours, speaks for itself. The accused orders his subordinates to employee this most heinous of weapons - a modified air-bomb - with the aim of inflicting the greatest casualties and material damage. As mentioned earlier, Your Honours, the Prosecution alleges that air-bombs designed to be dropped from aeroplanes were altered to enable them to be launched from the ground. These weapons, Your Honours, have no guidance system; in other words, they cannot be aimed. As such, they are entirely inappropriate for deployment into heavily populated urban areas, precisely where the accused ordered his subordinates to deploy them, Hrasnica and Sokolovic colony, residential areas. The Prosecution will present throughout this case extensive evidence of devastating consequences of the launch of air-bombs targeting the civilian population of Sarajevo. I would like to conclude the presentation of these four documents by showing you one of the protest letters addressed directly to the accused, and I have already briefly referred to the letter a moment ago. The document is dated the 30th of June, 1995. It's under the auspices of UNPROFOR, as you can see from the letterhead. 65 ter number, I should add, is 2491, and it was drafted by then-acting UNPROFOR Sector Sarajevo commander, the highest military official in Sarajevo from the United Nations, Colonel Robert Meille. And he tells Dragomir Milosevic: "On the 28th and 29th June, 1995, the Bosnian Serb forces of the Romanija Corps launched several attacks on civilian targets in the city of Sarajevo, using very powerful bombs as well as heavy artillery." Then he lists three specific targets that were hit all in residential areas. The letter continues, Your Honours: "This ill-considered and irresponsible escalation continued on the evening of 29 June when three high-power projectiles struck the PTT building, the HQ of commander Sector Sarajevo." It continues: "The seriousness of the events of the past 48 hours obliges me to remind both you and your officers most earnestly of your moral and legal obligation to adhere to the Geneva Convention as well as the agreements and assurances made to the peacekeeping forces. Protocol I of the Geneva Convention states, particularly in Section 2, Article 85, that deliberate attacks on the civilian population constitute a serious breach of the convention, rendering their perpetrators liable to trial by an international court." The letter concludes: "I strongly protest against these bombardments carried under -- carried out on your orders, and I demand that you immediately halt all attacks directed at either the civilian population or UNPROFOR." I really have no comment, Mr. President, other than to say that the letter was done both in English and B/C/S or Serbian, the language the accused perfectly understood. Let me address a few issues, Mr. President, about the Defence case so far as we are aware of it at this point in time. We only received a brief pre-trial brief, but there were a couple of points raised there, at least one which I would like to address, Mr. President. The Prosecution underscores that at all times the SRK and the accused had to abide by the we will-known tenet of conduct of hostilities principles and the bedrock of international humanitarian law, that civilians may not be the object of attack. And you have just seen a letter by Colonel Meille, reminding the accused of his obligations. This obligation, Mr. President, Your Honours, did not change or diminish depending on whether the ABiH, the defending forces of Sarajevo, themselves perpetrated wrong-doing, such as firing mortars or other heavy weapons into Bosnian Serb areas where civilians were hit. This fact could not entitle the accused and his subordinates to do likewise. There can be no tu quoque defence. The Prosecution accepts that the ABiH had sniping resources and heavy weapons, and particularly mortar weapons, and there was indeed a legitimate conflict ongoing in Sarajevo. Having said that, Prosecution will bring evidence that shows that at any time did the ABiH fire shells from within the confrontation lines at their own people, the persons they were supposed to defend. The Prosecution also accepts that on some occasions the ABiH may have fired mortars from within the hospital grounds of the Kosevo hospital; however, Mr. President, Your Honours, this would not have entitled the accused to send in barrage of shells at the hospital complex in retaliation. Typically, where hospitals are used to commit military acts, they would lose their protection under international humanitarian law only after due warning and a reasonable time-limit to cease military activities. But once the attack ceases, the hospital would revert to its status as a civilian target. In any event, in relation to the Kosevo hospital, the institution comprised a series of buildings in a large complex and so if mobile mortars were used from a small part of the ground, this would not give the SRK licence to fire shells on to the whole target, where the anticipated civilian casualties would have been excessive to any military advantage gained. According to the Defence pre-trial brief, Your Honours, the accused appears to raise the defence of alibi, specifically stating that from the 10th August, 1995, through to the 15th September, 1995, 45 days, he was not present in the Sarajevo theatre, but rather in Belgrade undergoing medical treatment. Even if the Prosecution were to accept this, we have seen no direct evidence of this yet, it does not affect the guilt of the accused. This case, Your Honours, does not concern crimes committed within a month period -- within a one-month period, but rather a campaign of shelling and sniping that took place over an extended period of time during which the accused created the conditions conducive for the commission of crimes through direct orders, as we have seen them, to attack civilians and omissions to act when those crimes were committed. By the time he would have left the theatre, the lawless environment was in place, and given the free reign the accused had permitted his subordinates to shell and snipe civilians, any crimes committed during the period of absence, especially the attack on the Sarajevo marketplace on 28th August 1995 are a direct result of the accused's actions and omissions. Further, when the accused returned just after the NATO strikes as a result of the market attack, the Prosecution will bring evidence to show that no steps were taken by the accused to initiate an investigation or to punish the perpetrators. Your Honours, the Prosecution's case is that the accused is individually criminally responsible for ordering and planning the crimes contained in the amended indictment. He implemented and/or further ordered the campaign of shelling or sniping civilians in order to primarily spread terror among the population -- civilian population of Sarajevo. It is the Prosecution's case that the accused inherited a pre- existing strategy of deliberate sniping and shelling of civilians. While this campaign or strategy was inherited, it was fine-tuned and ruthlessly implemented and perpetuated by Commander Stanislav Galic and, when he took over, the accused, Dragomir Milosevic. During the tenure of General Galic, as we know, the accused was brigade commander and, critically, the Chief of Staff of the SRK. During his time as Chief of Staff, the Prosecution will show that by virtue of this position he would have been privy to all decisions and issues pertaining to military operations and the commanding of the corps. The accused, therefore, when he became commander on 10th August 1994, clearly knew of the campaign against the civilian population. Through direct orders down the chain of command of his tightly- run and professional army corps, the accused furthered the campaign of attacks against the civilian population. The characteristics of the campaign remained the same as before, but with the introduction of modified air-bombs into the SRK arsenal, it was carried out with more destructive force and terror than ever. The Prosecution will present ample documentary evidence of direct orders from the accused related to the obtaining, deployment, and launching of modified air-bombs that prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused called the shots when it came to the use of these weapons. In one such order which we will present to Your Honours in trial, the accused orders for the deployment of 50 air-bombs. The Prosecution will bring direct and circumstantial evidence that the accused planned the firing of these and other heavy weapons, as well as the firing of direct-fire small-arms weapons against civilian targets. Even in the absence of further written orders directing the campaign against civilians, it will be clear from the evidence that the campaign of attacks against the civilians of Sarajevo continued, despite the anti-sniping agreement of 14th August 1994 and numerous protests from the UN and the international community. One UN military commander will be called before Your Honours and give evidence that in a six-month period, he protested to senior VRS commanders, including the accused, no fewer than 50 times about the sniping and shelling of civilians. The evidence of the pattern and the scale of the campaign will emerge through the testimony of surviving victims, UN monitors, and other eyewitnesses that will establish a convincing case based on direct and circumstantial evidence that civilians were deliberately targeted and that the accused exercised effective control over his infantry and artillery assets, in particular the modified air-bombs. Also, the Prosecution's case rests upon the inevitable and inescapable conclusion that the targeting of civilians by sniping and shelling could not have happened for so long and in a fashion which was observed to be responsive to his actions unless the accused had ordered it in the first place. As mentioned earlier, the Prosecution will bring evidence that the accused was repeatedly warned about civilian casualties as a result of sniping and shelling, but they continued, nevertheless, for the 15 months or so that the accused was in command. The accused could have been taken steps to prevent the attacks or discipline or punish his soldiers, but he did not, leaving the only inference that he had directly ordered the campaign. Dragomir Milosevic's position of effective control will prove to be indisputable. The Prosecution will show that from the time he took over the command of the SRK, he instituted a tight reign on the corps, from ordering his subordinates to preparing firing positions and monitor firing components to instituting regular meetings with his brigade officers. He had, at all times, the material about to prevent the commission of crimes and to investigate and punish his subordinates for the commission of crimes. He certainly had the power and material ability to investigate and to punish. Evidence will be presented that he did, indeed, initiate disciplinary measures against his soldiers like handing down prison sentences for deserters and similar offences. Yet, at the same time, the accused did never initiate any steps in his powers to investigate the crimes committed by his subordinates against the civilian population in Sarajevo. In conclusion Mr. President, Your Honours, General Milosevic held one of the highest military positions in the Army of Republika Srpska. When he assumed command of the SRK in August 1994, he inherited a pre- existing campaign to target civilians, of which he was aware by his prior positions. During his tenure as corps commander, the accused not only failed to prevent the campaign of attacks against civilians but also failed to punish the perpetrators. To the contrary, he continued the campaign of terror against the city of Sarajevo and its population. As mentioned, Mr. President and Your Honours, I would like to conclude the Prosecution's opening statement by showing a few contemporaneous video-clips. Let me clarify, as I have done before, that it's the Prosecution's case that the campaign of shelling and sniping against the civilian population is a continuous activity, starting in summer 1992 and spreading over 44 months into winter 1995. Therefore, Your Honours, the Prosecution will lead evidence that covers the campaign's entirety rather than specifically to the indictment period, which corresponds to the accused's tenure as corps commander of the SRK. Indeed, the collage of video-clips will predate the indictment period as well as portray events during it. It's only six minutes, by the way. The reasons are three-fold. Firstly, it is the Prosecution's case - and I say it for the third time - that the accused inherited a pre-existing strategy of deliberate sniping and shelling of civilians. Secondly, the characteristics of the campaign before and during his tenure are essentially identical. Thirdly, I mean to place the accused's actions in their proper historical context. Fourthly, by virtue of his prior positions, the accused is put on notice about the ongoing campaign he inherited. But I repeat, Your Honours, the accused is only accountable for the responsibilities which fell to him as a result of his period as the commander of the SRK. These clips, Mr. President and Your Honours, will provide you with a realtime impression of how it was. The first few clips are from the pre-indictment period. It starts with pre-war images of Sarajevo, the situation it was as described by Alex Whiting. Then shows images of the beginning of the campaign, during which the accused already had senior positions within the SRK. You will see some fabulous vantage positions the SRK had over the city showing that Sarajevo was at the mercy of the snipers and gunners. All war-related clips will illustrate to you the way sniping and shelling affected life; for instance, as trams were hit. And the clips will show, in particular, children as victims of this terror. You will also see footage from the Markale II massacre of 28th August 1995, exchanges shelling incident number 23, that cost the lives of so many people. The last clip, Your Honours, concerns Prosecution's scheduled incident number 5, sniping, the crime that occurred on the 14th November 1994 in front of the museum -- the national museum. That's the incident, Your Honours, whose characteristics I have explained to you earlier today in some detail showing 360-degree, you saw Mrs. Sokolovic talking to the investigator. Now, Your Honours, you will see the way it looked on the day it happened only seconds after the 7-year-old boy Nermin was shot by a sniper. The Prosecution wishes to draw your attention specifically to the rescue effort and the ongoing shooting which continued throughout.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.
